cards.front: In the embryo cells studied, what determines where cytokinesis begins?
cards.back: Anaphase microtubules place a band of active RhoA. If the microtubules move, the RhoA band moves first and the furrow follows.
cards.quote: In the embryo cells studied, the cut goes where the anaphase microtubules place a band of active RhoA.

cards.front: After mitosis sorts the chromosomes, what three jobs remain for cell division?
cards.back: Place the cut, make the cut, and give each daughter a working share of the cell's contents.
cards.quote: The cell has three jobs left: place the cut, make the cut, and give each daughter a working share of what it contains.

cards.front: Two spindles lie side by side in a ring-shaped embryo cell. Asters from different spindles face across a gap with no spindle between them. Where should an extra furrow form, and what would it show?
cards.back: A furrow should form between the facing asters. It would show that facing microtubule asters can mark a furrow site without a complete spindle joining them.
cards.quote: Furrows formed across each spindle and also in the gap between the facing asters

cards.front: The enzyme that switches RhoA on at the equator is {{c1::Ect2}}.
cards.back: Ect2 is a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor.
cards.quote: Ect2 is the enzyme that switches RhoA on.

cards.front: How does Ect2 switch RhoA on?
cards.back: As a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor, Ect2 makes RhoA release GDP, allowing abundant cellular GTP to replace it.
cards.quote: It is a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor (GEF): it makes RhoA let go of its GDP, and GTP, which is plentiful in the cell, takes its place.

cards.front: The dense bundle of overlapping microtubules between separating chromosomes is the {{c1::spindle midzone}}.
cards.back: It is the most prominent site of microtubule overlap.
cards.quote: The most prominent overlap is the spindle midzone, the dense bundle of overlapping microtubules between the separating chromosomes

cards.front: How does centralspindlin connect anaphase microtubules to RhoA activation?
cards.back: Centralspindlin gathers at overlapping microtubules, binds Ect2 at anaphase, and helps activate it; Ect2 then switches RhoA on.
cards.quote: At anaphase, centralspindlin binds Ect2 and helps activate it.

cards.front: Ect2 is depleted from cultured human cells, but their chromosomes still separate normally. What happens after mitosis, and why?
cards.back: Many cells remain binucleate with doubled DNA. Without Ect2, they fail to concentrate RhoA, actin, and myosin at the equator, so the furrow fails.
cards.quote: many cells fail to concentrate RhoA, actin filaments and myosin at the equator, their furrows fail

cards.front: Why is the equatorial RhoA band not simply a map of every microtubule overlap?
cards.back: The band reflects the microtubule cue, but how its sharp boundaries form remains debated.
cards.quote: The band reflects this microtubule cue, but it is not a simple print of where microtubules overlap

cards.front: A drug blocks actin assembly in an embryo, yet an equatorial band of GTP-bound RhoA still appears. Which causal order survives this result?
cards.back: RhoA activation is upstream of actin assembly: the RhoA band can form even when actin assembly is blocked.
cards.quote: Move the microtubules, and the band moves first; the furrow follows.

cards.front: A spindle is displaced during furrowing; the active-RhoA band relocates before the furrow. Combined with Ect2 depletion, what pathway is supported?
cards.back: Anaphase microtubules position centralspindlin and Ect2, Ect2 activates equatorial RhoA, and RhoA drives the actin-myosin furrow. Each perturbation supports a different link in this sequence.
cards.quote: Two proteins relay the microtubules' position to it. Ect2 is the enzyme that switches RhoA on.

cards.front: How do formins and nonmuscle myosin II make an animal-cell furrow ingress?
cards.back: Formins build the ring's actin filaments, and myosin II pulls within the ring so it tightens and draws the furrow inward.
cards.quote: The ring the film built under the band, of formin-made actin filaments and nonmuscle myosin II, pulls the furrow in

cards.front: The separate, final cut that divides the intercellular bridge is called {{c1::abscission}}.
cards.back: It occurs after furrow ingression.
cards.quote: Abscission, the final cut, is a separate, later step.

cards.front: What is the midbody?
cards.back: A dense plug of overlapping microtubules and proteins at the center of the intercellular bridge, left from the spindle midzone.
cards.quote: At its centre sits the midbody, a dense plug of overlapping microtubules and proteins left from the spindle midzone.

cards.front: A cultured human cell finishes furrow ingression, but ESCRT-III cannot assemble in its intercellular bridge. What happens and why?
cards.back: The bridge persists and abscission is delayed or fails. ESCRT-III normally forms membrane spirals that constrict and cut the bridge.
cards.quote: ESCRT-III, a set of proteins that polymerize into spirals on membranes, assembles in the bridge, constricts it and cuts it.

cards.front: Chromatin remains trapped in the intercellular bridge. What happens to abscission?
cards.back: The final cut can be delayed, preventing the bridge from being severed while chromatin remains inside it.
cards.quote: Chromatin left in the bridge can delay the cut.

cards.front: How can either an early Ect2 defect or a late abscission defect produce a tetraploid, binucleate cell?
cards.back: In the cultured human-cell experiment, Ect2 depletion causes many cells to fail furrowing; an abscission defect can let the bridge regress. Either route can leave one cell with two nuclei and doubled DNA.
cards.quote: If the cut fails, the bridge can regress and leave one cell with two nuclei and doubled DNA.

cards.front: Why does the prevalent mode of somatic plant cytokinesis build a cell plate instead of pinching inward?
cards.back: A plant cell lies inside a rigid wall, so it cannot pinch; new membrane begins centrally and grows outward to the old wall.
cards.quote: a plant cell cannot pinch, because it sits inside a rigid wall.
cards.section: Plants build a wall from the inside out

cards.front: In the prevalent mode of somatic plant cytokinesis, the microtubule-and-actin array that guides Golgi vesicles is the {{c1::phragmoplast}}.
cards.back: It forms between the two daughter nuclei.
cards.quote: The builder is the phragmoplast, an array of microtubules and actin filaments that forms between the two daughter nuclei.
cards.section: Plants build a wall from the inside out

cards.front: How does the phragmoplast produce a completed cell plate?
cards.back: It guides Golgi vesicles to the division plane; they fuse into a membrane compartment that expands sideways until it joins the parental wall.
cards.quote: It guides vesicles from the Golgi to the centre of the division plane.
cards.section: Plants build a wall from the inside out

cards.front: The Arabidopsis syntaxin-related protein needed for vesicle fusion at the division plane is {{c1::KNOLLE}}.
cards.back: It is a target-membrane SNARE-related protein.
cards.quote: KNOLLE, an Arabidopsis protein related to syntaxins, the target-membrane SNAREs you met in vesicle traffic, sits at the division plane.
cards.section: Plants build a wall from the inside out

cards.front: A plant mutant has incomplete walls. Electron micrographs show crowds of vesicles in the division plane. Does delivery or fusion most likely fail, and why?
cards.back: Fusion most likely fails. The vesicles reached the plane; a delivery defect would instead leave few vesicles there.
cards.quote: A block in delivery along the phragmoplast, or in Golgi production, would leave few vesicles in the plane; a fusion block would leave a crowd.
cards.section: Plants build a wall from the inside out

cards.front: What does the preprophase band do in many plant cells?
cards.back: Before mitosis, this cortical microtubule ring marks the future division plane and often helps orient division, then disappears.
cards.quote: Before mitosis, many plant cells build a preprophase band, a cortical ring of microtubules that marks the future division plane and then disappears.
cards.section: Plants build a wall from the inside out

cards.front: Cell A ingresses a furrow and leaves a microtubule-filled bridge. Cell B builds a central membrane compartment that expands to the parental wall. Identify each cell type and division machinery.
cards.back: A is an animal cell using a RhoA-directed actin-myosin ring, followed by abscission. B is a plant cell using a phragmoplast to build an outward-growing cell plate.
cards.quote: The plate expands sideways toward the parental cell surface, and cytokinesis is complete when it joins the old wall.
cards.section: Plants build a wall from the inside out

cards.front: Under independent 0.5 partitioning, one daughter's organelle count follows a {{c1::binomial distribution}}.
cards.back: This is a no-control null model.
cards.quote: The count in one daughter then follows a binomial distribution.

cards.front: What assumptions define the lesson's no-control model of organelle partition?
cards.back: Organelle units partition independently, and each has an equal 0.5 chance of entering either daughter.
cards.quote: This is one no-control null model, under the stated assumptions: independent units, equal chance of entering either daughter.

cards.front: Six independent organelle units each enter either daughter with probability 0.5. What is the probability that one daughter or the other gets none?
cards.back: P = 2 × 0.5^6 = 2/64 = 0.03125, or about 3.1%. The factor 2 counts either daughter being empty.
cards.quote: P(one daughter gets none) = 2 × 0.5^n

cards.front: One hundred independent organelle units partition with probability 0.5 per daughter. Find one daughter's mean and standard deviation, then give the approximate two-standard-deviation interval.
cards.back: Mean = 100 × 0.5 = 50. SD = sqrt(100 × 0.5 × 0.5) = 5. The interval is 50 ± 10, or 40–60 units.
cards.quote: Mean = 50. Standard deviation = square root of 25 = 5.

cards.front: Ten independent organelle units partition equally at random. What is the risk that either daughter receives none?
cards.back: P = 2 × 0.5^10 = 2/1024 = 0.001953, about 0.2%, or roughly one division in 500.
cards.quote: One division in five hundred leaves a daughter with none.

cards.front: Under independent 0.5 partitioning, what minimum number of organelle units makes the risk that either daughter gets none less than 0.1%?
cards.back: Use 2 × 0.5^n < 0.001. At n = 11, P = 0.0009766, about 0.098%, so 11 units is the minimum.
cards.quote: Each added unit halves the risk, so it falls below one in a thousand at n = 11

cards.front: Fifty organelle units should partition independently with an expected standard deviation of about 3.5, but 200 daughter pairs show a standard deviation of 1. What follows?
cards.back: Reject the coin-toss model: partitioning is much more even than expected. An equalizing mechanism fits, but the spread alone cannot identify it.
cards.quote: The data reject the coin-toss model. Its standard deviation is the square root of 12.5, about 3.5

cards.front: Why is random organelle partition safer for many independent units than for one connected network?
cards.back: The risk of an empty daughter halves with each independent unit. A connected network acts as one unit, so it must fragment or be actively segregated.
cards.quote: Conclusion: chance is safe only for many independent units.

cards.front: Two partition mechanisms both give daughters a mean of 25 organelle units. How can observations distinguish random partition from symmetric equalization?
cards.back: Compare the spread or full distribution. Random independent partition predicts SD about 3.5 for 50 units; a much smaller spread supports equalization even though the means match.
cards.quote: both this model and a symmetric equalizing mechanism have a mean of 25, so the much smaller spread is what rejects the coin-toss model

cards.front: How can an asymmetric cultured-cell division test whether working Golgi stacks require the spindle for inheritance?
cards.back: Send the whole spindle into a karyoplast and none into a cytoplast. Then test the cytoplast for Golgi stacks and secretion; finding functional stacks there would refute strict spindle-only inheritance.
cards.quote: Induce asymmetric divisions that send the entire spindle, with the chromosomes, into one product (a karyoplast) and none into the other (a cytoplast).

cards.front: Why inject mRNA for a membrane reporter into a spindle-free cytoplast in the Golgi-partition experiment?
cards.back: Surface arrival of the reporter tests whether the inherited Golgi stacks support a working secretory pathway, not merely whether Golgi markers are present.
cards.quote: Test function: inject mRNA for a membrane reporter such as CD8 and ask whether the protein reaches the cell surface

cards.front: A spindle-free cytoplast contains functional Golgi stacks but no Golgi ribbon. Tubulin alone fails to restore the ribbon; Golgi extract plus tubulin succeeds. What is the narrow conclusion?
cards.back: Working stacks can be inherited without the spindle. Tubulin alone is insufficient for ribbon reassembly, whereas Golgi extract plus tubulin can restore it.
cards.quote: Tubulin alone did not restore a ribbon; Golgi extract plus tubulin did.

cards.front: What limits the conclusion from the engineered PtK1 Golgi-partition experiment?
cards.back: It used an engineered division in one cell line; it neither excludes all spindle use by Golgi membranes nor resolves passage of Golgi components through the ER.
cards.quote: This is an engineered division in one cell line.

cards.front: What three mechanisms may help keep the equatorial RhoA band narrow?
cards.back: Midzone delivery of Ect2, polar inhibition by astral microtubules, and rapid cycling of RhoA.
cards.quote: Three mechanisms may all contribute to the sharp edge, in different proportions in different cells

cards.front: Why should the spindle-positioning rule from embryo cells not be treated as universal for all animal cells?
cards.back: Some animal cells add other cues; in Drosophila neuroblasts, a polarity pathway can position the furrow independently of the spindle.
cards.quote: In Drosophila neuroblasts, which divide asymmetrically, a polarity pathway can position a furrow independently of the spindle
cards.section: A furrow placed without the spindle

cards.front: Mitochondria gather less at the furrow after Miro-1 is disrupted, but inheritance looks normal. What can and cannot be concluded?
cards.back: Miro-1-dependent positioning was perturbed, but this experiment did not show an inheritance defect. Moving an organelle and changing daughter shares are separate claims.
cards.quote: Moving an organelle and changing its shares are separate claims
